Computable answers are re-derived in tools/batch_010/computer.py (bit fields, octal, rotation, a processor simulation, priority scheduling, TTL, set-associative mapping, TLB access time, printer bitmap, stop-and-wait, IPv4 fragmentation, toy RSA, SQL in sqlite3 with > ALL checked in Python, and Excel PROPER / EOMONTH / DATEDIF checked against Microsoft's own examples or definitions). Facts were checked on 2026-11-05 on RFC, Microsoft, MDN, man7, GNU, OWASP, NIST, IEEE, ICANN, IBM, RBI, DARPA, CERN, US Census Bureau, LibreOffice, Google and Wikipedia pages.

stimuli.title: Status word of a note-sorting machine
stimuli.content:
A currency note-sorting machine in a cash-processing centre reports its state to the controller as one 16-bit status word, shown in hexadecimal. The bits are numbered 15 (leftmost) to 0 (rightmost):

| Bits | Field | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| 15-13 | Mode | 3-bit operating mode |
| 12-5 | Count | 8-bit unsigned number of notes in the current bundle |
| 4-0 | Error | 5-bit error code |

The status word received at 10:42 is **9C5A** (hexadecimal).
stimuli.solution: 9C5A = 1001 1100 0101 1010 in binary. Mode = bits 15-13 = 100 = 4; Count = bits 12-5 = 1110 0010 = 226; Error = bits 4-0 = 11010 = 26. As an unsigned number the word is 40,026, which is 116132 in octal. Rotating the word left by 4 bits moves the leading hex digit 9 to the end: C5A9.

stimuli.title: Program on a teaching accumulator processor
stimuli.content:
A bank's IT training lab uses a simple processor with one register for data, the accumulator (ACC), and a program counter (PC) that always holds the address of the NEXT instruction to fetch. Each instruction occupies one memory word and is fetched with ONE memory access. LOAD, SUB and STORE each make ONE further memory access for their data; JUMPNEG and HALT make none.

| Address | Instruction | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| 100 | LOAD 200 | ACC <- contents of address 200 |
| 101 | SUB 201 | ACC <- ACC - contents of address 201 |
| 102 | JUMPNEG 106 | If ACC < 0, continue at address 106 |
| 103 | LOAD 200 | ACC <- contents of 200 |
| 104 | STORE 202 | Contents of 202 <- ACC |
| 105 | HALT | Stop |
| 106 | LOAD 201 | ACC <- contents of 201 |
| 107 | STORE 202 | Contents of 202 <- ACC |
| 108 | HALT | Stop |

Before the run, address 200 holds 45, address 201 holds 60 and address 202 holds 0. Execution starts at 100.
stimuli.solution: 45 - 60 = -15 is negative, so the jump is taken: the instructions run are 100, 101, 102, 106, 107 and 108, and 60 is stored in 202. The program stores the larger of the two numbers. Memory accesses = 6 instruction fetches + 4 data accesses (LOAD, SUB, LOAD, STORE) = 10.

stimuli.title: Overnight batch jobs on an end-of-day server
stimuli.content:
A bank's end-of-day (EOD) server has one CPU and runs four batch jobs. Times are in minutes after the batch window opens. A SMALLER priority number means a HIGHER priority. A job's turnaround time = completion time - arrival time; its waiting time = turnaround time - burst time. Ignore context-switch time.

| Job | Task | Arrival time | CPU burst | Priority |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| J1 | Interest posting | 0 | 8 | 3 |
| J2 | ATM cash reconciliation | 1 | 4 | 1 |
| J3 | Statement generation | 2 | 9 | 4 |
| J4 | Loan EMI debit | 3 | 5 | 2 |
stimuli.solution: Non-preemptive priority: J1 runs 0-8 (only job present at 0), then J2 8-12, J4 12-17, J3 17-26; turnaround times 8, 11, 24 and 14, average 14.25 minutes. Preemptive priority: J1 0-1, J2 1-5, J4 5-10, J1 10-17, J3 17-26; waiting times J1 9, J2 0, J3 15, J4 2, average 6.5 minutes.

stimuli.title: DNS records seen by a branch PC
stimuli.content:
A branch technician looks up the bank's names with a DNS tool and gets these resource records (TTL in seconds; all records are class IN):

| Name | TTL | Type | Data |
|---|---|---|---|
| netbanking.bank.example | 300 | CNAME | web.bank.example |
| web.bank.example | 300 | A | 203.0.113.25 |
| web.bank.example | 300 | AAAA | 2001:db8:10::25 |
| bank.example | 3600 | MX | 10 mail1.bank.example |
| bank.example | 3600 | MX | 20 mail2.bank.example |
| bank.example | 86400 | NS | ns1.bank.example |
| bank.example | 86400 | NS | ns2.bank.example |
| 25.113.0.203.in-addr.arpa | 3600 | PTR | web.bank.example |
stimuli.solution: netbanking.bank.example is an alias of web.bank.example, whose IPv4 address is 203.0.113.25 (A record) and IPv6 address is 2001:db8:10::25 (AAAA record). Mail goes first to mail1 (MX preference 10, lower is preferred). ns1 and ns2 are the authoritative name servers of the zone. The PTR record under in-addr.arpa maps the IP address back to a name. TTL tells resolvers how many seconds they may cache each record.

questions.subject: Computer Knowledge
questions.question_text: Refer to the note-sorting machine. What is the status word 9C5A when it is read as one unsigned decimal number?

solution.explanation: Multiply each hex digit by its place value (powers of 16): 9 x 4096 + 12 x 256 + 5 x 16 + 10 x 1 = 36,864 + 3,072 + 80 + 10 = 40,026.
solution.why_others_wrong: The other values come from slips in the place values or in the values of the letter digits C and A.

questions.subject: Computer Knowledge
questions.question_text: Refer to the note-sorting machine. How many notes does the Count field (bits 12-5) report?

solution.explanation: 9C5A = 1001 1100 0101 1010. Bits 15-13 are 100 (Mode) and bits 4-0 are 11010 (Error); the eight bits in between, bits 12 to 5, are 1110 0010 = 128 + 64 + 32 + 2 = 226. (In code: (word >> 5) AND FF.)
steps: Shift right by 5 (drop the Error bits): 100 1110 0010
solution.why_others_wrong: 197 is C5, the middle two hex digits, which do not line up with bits 12-5. 90 is 5A, the lowest byte. 113 is the field taken one place too far left (bits 13-6).

questions.subject: Computer Knowledge
questions.question_text: Refer to the note-sorting machine. A legacy log prints the status word in octal (base 8). What does it print for 9C5A?

solution.explanation: Write the word in binary and regroup into 3-bit groups from the right: 1 001 110 001 011 010 -> 1 1 6 1 3 2 = 116132 (octal). Check: 1 x 32768 + 1 x 4096 + 6 x 512 + 1 x 64 + 3 x 8 + 2 = 40,026.
steps: Group in threes from the right: 1 001 110 001 011 010
solution.shortcut: Hex -> binary -> octal by regrouping 4-bit groups into 3-bit groups.
solution.why_others_wrong: 116232 misreads one group (001 as 010). 470550 groups the bits in threes from the LEFT instead of the right. 9C5A is the hexadecimal form, and C and A are not octal digits.

questions.subject: Computer Knowledge
questions.question_text: Refer to the note-sorting machine. The controller ROTATES the 16-bit word 9C5A LEFT by 4 bit positions (a circular shift: bits leaving on the left re-enter on the right). What is the result in hexadecimal?

solution.explanation: Rotating a 16-bit word left by 4 bits moves each hex digit one place left, and the leading digit 9 wraps round to the right end: 9C5A -> C5A9. A logical left shift would instead fill the right end with zeros (C5A0).
steps: Digits move one place left: C 5 A _
The 9 that left on the left re-enters: C5A9
solution.shortcut: Rotate by 4 bits = rotate the hex digits by one place.
solution.why_others_wrong: C5A0 is a logical left shift (zeros enter). 09C5 is a logical right shift by 4. A9C5 is a rotation to the RIGHT by 4 bits.

questions.subject: Computer Knowledge
questions.question_text: A value is written in octal (base 8) as 17. What is its value in decimal?

solution.explanation: In base 8 the place values are 8 and 1: 1 x 8 + 7 x 1 = 15.
solution.why_others_wrong: 17 reads the digits as if they were decimal. 8 just adds the digits 1 + 7. 23 uses 16 as the place value of the first digit (that would be hexadecimal 17).

questions.subject: Computer Knowledge
questions.question_text: A test asks which of these four values is the LARGEST. Which one is it?

solution.concept: Comparing numbers written in different bases
solution.why_others_wrong: 3E is 62, 75 octal is 61 and 60 decimal is 60, all smaller than 63.

questions.subject: Computer Knowledge
questions.question_text: In 1617 the Scottish mathematician John Napier published a manually operated calculating aid made of numbered rods, used to work out products and quotients. What is this device called?

solution.explanation: Napier's bones are a set of numbered rods laid side by side so that multiplication can be done by adding the digits shown, and division by repeated steps. Napier published them in 1617.
steps: John Napier, 1617, rods for products and quotients -> Napier's bones
solution.why_others_wrong: The Pascaline was Blaise Pascal's geared adding machine (1640s). The Difference Engine was Charles Babbage's design for tabulating polynomials. The abacus is an ancient bead frame, not Napier's invention.

fact_checks.claim: Napier's bones is a manually operated calculating device created by John Napier of Merchiston for the calculation of products and quotients; Napier published his version in 1617.

questions.subject: Computer Knowledge
questions.question_text: The PCs, ATMs and mobile phones used by a bank all represent data as discrete binary values (0s and 1s) and process them by counting rather than by measuring a continuous quantity. On the basis of how they work, such computers are classified as:

solution.explanation: Computers are classified as analog (measure continuously varying quantities), digital (work with discrete digits, in practice binary) or hybrid (combine both). Everyday PCs, ATMs and phones are digital computers.
solution.why_others_wrong: Analog computers measure continuous quantities such as voltage. Hybrid computers combine analog and digital parts. Optical computing is a research area, not the class of these devices.

questions.subject: Computer Knowledge
questions.question_text: The US Census Bureau signed a contract for a computer in March 1951 and held its dedication ceremony in June 1951; the Bureau describes it as the first successful civilian computer. Which computer was it?

solution.explanation: UNIVAC I (Universal Automatic Computer), built by the company of J. Presper Eckert and John Mauchly, went to the US Census Bureau in 1951 and became the first successful civilian (commercial) computer in the United States. Like other first-generation machines it used vacuum tubes.
steps: Census Bureau, 1951, first successful civilian computer -> UNIVAC I
solution.why_others_wrong: ENIAC (1945) was built for the US Army's ballistics work. EDSAC (1949) was a stored-program computer at Cambridge University. The IBM 701 was IBM's first commercial scientific computer, not the Census Bureau's 1951 machine.

fact_checks.claim: The Census Bureau signed a contract for UNIVAC I on 31 March 1951, held a dedication in June 1951 and calls it the first successful civilian computer.

questions.subject: Computer Knowledge
questions.question_text: Which machine, built from scratch by C-DAC and delivered in 1991, was the first of the PARAM series and is remembered as India's first indigenous supercomputer?

solution.explanation: C-DAC was set up in 1988 to build an indigenous supercomputer. The PARAM 8000, a parallel machine built from transputers, was delivered in 1991 and was the first machine of the PARAM series.
solution.why_others_wrong: PARAM Padma (2002), PARAM Yuva and PARAM Siddhi-AI are later machines of the series.

fact_checks.claim: Wikipedia's PARAM article: the PARAM 8000 was the first machine in the series and was built from scratch; a 64-node machine was delivered in August 1991; its cited C-DAC item says this gave India her first indigenous supercomputer in 1991.

questions.subject: Computer Knowledge
questions.question_text: Refer to the accumulator processor. What does the program counter hold immediately after the JUMPNEG instruction at address 102 has finished executing?

solution.explanation: During the fetch of the instruction at 102 the PC is advanced to 103. ACC holds 45 - 60 = -15, which is negative, so JUMPNEG overwrites the PC with its target 106. The next instruction fetched is therefore at 106.
solution.why_others_wrong: 103 would be the PC if the jump were not taken. 102 is the address of the jump itself. 107 is one instruction too far: the PC points to the next instruction to fetch, which is 106.

questions.subject: Computer Knowledge
questions.question_text: Refer to the accumulator processor. When the program halts, what value is stored at address 202?

solution.explanation: LOAD 200 puts 45 in ACC; SUB 201 makes it 45 - 60 = -15; the result is negative, so control jumps to 106, where LOAD 201 puts 60 in ACC and STORE 202 writes 60 to address 202. The program stores the larger of the two numbers.
solution.why_others_wrong: -15 is the difference, which is never stored. 45 would be stored only if the jump were not taken. 15 is the size of the difference.

questions.subject: Computer Knowledge
questions.question_text: Refer to the accumulator processor. Counting both instruction fetches and data accesses, how many memory accesses does the whole run make, up to and including the HALT that stops it?

solution.concept: Instruction cycle: fetch and operand accesses
solution.explanation: Six instructions run (100, 101, 102, 106, 107, 108), each needing one fetch = 6 accesses. Of these, LOAD 200, SUB 201, LOAD 201 and STORE 202 each make one data access = 4. Total = 10.
steps: Data accesses: LOAD, SUB, LOAD, STORE = 4
solution.why_others_wrong: 6 counts only the fetches and 4 only the data accesses. 9 forgets the fetch of the final HALT.

questions.subject: Computer Knowledge
questions.question_text: Refer to the accumulator processor. If address 200 held 75 instead of 45 (address 201 still holds 60), what would address 202 hold when the program halts?

options.text: 75, because the program now reloads 75 and stores it
0, because the program halts before any STORE

solution.explanation: 75 - 60 = 15 is not negative, so JUMPNEG does not jump. Execution continues at 103: LOAD 200 puts 75 back into ACC, STORE 202 writes 75 and HALT at 105 stops the run. In both cases the program stores the larger of the two numbers.
solution.why_others_wrong: 15 would be stored only if there were no LOAD at 103 to reload the original value. 60 is stored only on the jump path. A STORE does run (at 104) before the HALT.
solution.final_answer: Option A: 75, because the program now reloads 75 and stores it

questions.subject: Computer Knowledge
questions.question_text: An old dot-matrix printer in a branch has a wide 25-pin connector and was designed for the PC port that sends 8 bits at a time over separate wires, often called the LPT port. Which port is this?

solution.explanation: The parallel (LPT, Centronics) port sends the 8 bits of a byte simultaneously over 8 data wires and was the standard printer port before USB. A serial (COM) port sends bits one after another.
steps: 8 bits at a time, printer, LPT -> parallel port
solution.why_others_wrong: A serial port sends one bit at a time. PS/2 is a small round port for keyboards and mice. HDMI carries digital video and audio.

questions.subject: Computer Knowledge
questions.question_text: A technician building desktops for a bank buys a cabinet, a power supply and a motherboard that all follow the same standard, so that the board's mounting holes, rear connector panel and power connectors fit together. What is this standard size and layout of a motherboard called?

solution.explanation: A form factor such as ATX, micro-ATX or mini-ITX fixes the board's dimensions, mounting-hole positions, rear I/O panel position and power connectors, so that compatible cases and power supplies fit.
steps: Physical size and layout standard -> form factor
solution.why_others_wrong: The chipset controls data flow between components. The socket type decides which processors fit. Bus width is the number of bits a bus carries at once.
solution.final_answer: Option A: Form factor (for example ATX)

questions.subject: Computer Knowledge
questions.question_text: To make a trading-desk PC faster, a technician sets its processor to run above the clock speed at which the manufacturer rated it, which increases heat and can make the system unstable. What is this practice called?

solution.explanation: Overclocking runs a component such as the CPU or RAM above its rated clock frequency to gain speed, at the cost of more heat, more power use and possible instability.
solution.why_others_wrong: Thermal throttling is the opposite: the processor lowers its own speed when it gets too hot. Hyper-threading runs two threads per core. Pipelining overlaps the stages of several instructions.

questions.subject: Computer Knowledge
questions.question_text: A small branch office wants a word processor, spreadsheet and presentation program that can be used legally at no cost and whose source code anyone may study and improve. Which suite fits this need?

options.text: A 30-day trial version of a paid office suite (shareware)
A cracked copy of a paid office suite

solution.explanation: LibreOffice is free and open-source software: it costs nothing and its source code can be studied and improved by anyone. It includes Writer (word processor), Calc (spreadsheet) and Impress (presentations).
steps: No cost + source open to study and improve -> open-source suite such as LibreOffice
solution.why_others_wrong: Microsoft 365 is proprietary and paid by subscription. A trial version must be bought after the trial. A cracked copy is pirated software and illegal.
solution.final_answer: Option A: LibreOffice (free and open-source software)

fact_checks.claim: LibreOffice describes itself as free and open source software, so anyone can study how it works and add improvements; it includes Writer, Calc and Impress.

questions.subject: Computer Knowledge
questions.question_text: A bank pays a fixed fee every year for each officer who uses an analytics tool. If the bank stops paying, the officers lose the right to use it, but while it pays it always gets the latest version. What type of licence is this?

solution.explanation: Under a subscription licence the customer pays a recurring (monthly or yearly) fee for the right to use the software, usually with updates included; the right ends when the payments stop.
steps: Recurring fee + rights end when payment stops -> subscription
solution.why_others_wrong: A perpetual licence is paid for once and the bought version may be used for ever. Freeware costs nothing. Public domain software has no copyright restrictions at all.

questions.subject: Computer Knowledge
questions.question_text: A trainee says, 'I programmed the branch's web page in HTML.' His trainer points out that HTML is not a programming language. Why?

options.text: HTML can only be run after it is compiled into machine code by the browser's compiler
HTML is an assembly language for the browser's processor
HTML is a markup language: its tags describe the structure of content, and it has no variables, conditions or loops of its own
HTML is a database query language like SQL

solution.explanation:
HTML (HyperText Markup Language) marks up content with tags such as

,

and to show its structure. It cannot by itself make decisions, repeat steps or calculate; logic on a web page comes from a programming language such as JavaScript.
steps: Tags describe structure; no logic of its own
solution.why_others_wrong: Browsers parse HTML; they do not compile it into machine code. HTML is not an assembly language. It is not a query language either.
solution.final_answer: Option C: HTML is a markup language: its tags describe the structure of content, and it has no variables, conditions or loops of its own

questions.subject: Computer Knowledge
questions.question_text:
Consider this pseudocode:

procedure addBonus(x)
    x = x + 100
end procedure

b = 500
addBonus(b)
print b

What is printed if the parameter is passed BY VALUE, and what if it is passed BY REFERENCE?

options.text: 600 with pass by value; 500 with pass by reference
500 with pass by value; 600 with pass by reference

solution.concept: Parameter passing: by value and by reference
solution.explanation: With pass by value, x is a separate copy of b; changing x to 600 does not affect b, so 500 is printed. With pass by reference, x is another name for b itself, so the change makes b = 600 and 600 is printed.
steps: By value: x is a copy -> b stays 500
By reference: x refers to b -> b becomes 600
solution.why_others_wrong: The second option swaps the two mechanisms. The last two options ignore the difference between a copy and a reference.
solution.final_answer: Option B: 500 with pass by value; 600 with pass by reference

questions.subject: Computer Knowledge
questions.question_text:
In a language that uses short-circuit evaluation for AND, a program runs:

if count != 0 AND total / count > 1000 then
    print "High average"
end if

with count = 0 and total = 50000. What happens?

options.text: The condition is simply false and no division is performed, because count != 0 is false and AND stops there
The program crashes with a division-by-zero error
The condition is true, because total / 0 is treated as infinity
The compiler rejects the statement because it may divide by zero

solution.explanation: With short-circuit AND, the right-hand operand is evaluated only when the left-hand operand is true. Here count != 0 is false, so the whole condition is false and total / count is never computed; nothing is printed and no error occurs. This is why the zero check is written first.
steps: AND with false is false -> stop
solution.why_others_wrong: A crash would happen only if both operands were always evaluated. Division by zero is not treated as infinity in integer arithmetic, and it is never reached here. A compiler cannot know the run-time value of count, so it does not reject the statement.
solution.final_answer: Option A: The condition is simply false and no division is performed, because count != 0 is false and AND stops there

questions.subject: Computer Knowledge
questions.question_text: A fintech company modifies an open-source loan-calculator program licensed under the GNU Affero GPL (AGPL) and runs it on its own server, where customers use it through a web browser; the company never hands out copies of the program. What does the AGPL require?

options.text: Nothing, because the program is never distributed as a copy
Only the original author's copyright notice must be kept, as with the MIT licence
The company must pay a royalty to the Free Software Foundation
Users who interact with the modified program over the network must be able to get its modified source code

solution.explanation: Ordinary GPL obligations are triggered by distributing copies, so a program that only runs on a server escapes them. The AGPL closes this gap: if you run a modified version on a server and let users interact with it there, the server must also let them download the corresponding source code.
steps: Modified AGPL program + users interact over a network
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Nothing' describes the plain GPL server loophole that the AGPL was written to close. Keeping only a copyright notice is the permissive MIT model. Free-software licences do not charge royalties.
solution.final_answer: Option D: Users who interact with the modified program over the network must be able to get its modified source code

fact_checks.claim: The FSF explains that the AGPL adds one requirement to GPLv3: if you run a modified program on a server and let other users communicate with it there, your server must also allow them to download the source code of the modified version.

questions.subject: Computer Knowledge
questions.question_text: Refer to the EOD batch jobs. Under NON-preemptive priority scheduling, in what order do the jobs complete?

solution.explanation: At time 0 only J1 has arrived, so it starts and, being non-preemptive, runs to completion at 8. By then J2 (priority 1), J3 (4) and J4 (2) are all waiting; the highest priority, J2, runs 8-12, then J4 12-17, then J3 17-26.
solution.why_others_wrong: J2, J4, J1, J3 is the preemptive order (J2 interrupts J1). J1, J2, J3, J4 is first-come, first-served. J2, J1, J4, J3 assumes J2 was present at time 0.
solution.final_answer: Option C: J1, J2, J4, J3

questions.subject: Computer Knowledge
questions.question_text: Refer to the EOD batch jobs. Under NON-preemptive priority scheduling, what is the average turnaround time?

solution.explanation: Completion times: J1 8, J2 12, J4 17, J3 26. Turnaround = completion - arrival: J1 8 - 0 = 8, J2 12 - 1 = 11, J4 17 - 3 = 14, J3 26 - 2 = 24. Average = (8 + 11 + 14 + 24) / 4 = 57 / 4 = 14.25 minutes.
solution.why_others_wrong: 15.75 averages the completion times without subtracting arrival times. 7.75 is the average WAITING time under this schedule. 13 is the average turnaround under PREEMPTIVE priority.

questions.subject: Computer Knowledge
questions.question_text: Refer to the EOD batch jobs. If the scheduler is changed to PREEMPTIVE priority (a newly arrived job with a higher priority immediately takes the CPU from the running job), what is the average waiting time?

solution.explanation: J1 runs 0-1; J2 arrives at 1 with priority 1 and preempts it, running 1-5. At 5, J4 (priority 2) beats J1 (3) and J3 (4): J4 runs 5-10. J1 finishes its remaining 7 minutes 10-17, then J3 runs 17-26. Waiting = completion - arrival - burst: J1 17 - 0 - 8 = 9, J2 5 - 1 - 4 = 0, J4 10 - 3 - 5 = 2, J3 26 - 2 - 9 = 15. Average = 26 / 4 = 6.5 minutes.
solution.why_others_wrong: 7.75 is the average waiting time WITHOUT preemption. 4 and 9 come from leaving out a job's waiting time or counting J1's wait as only 1 minute.

questions.subject: Computer Knowledge
questions.question_text: A clerk copied several account numbers one after another and now wants to paste one she copied earlier, not the latest one. Which Windows keyboard shortcut opens the clipboard history so she can choose it?

solution.explanation: Windows logo key + V opens the clipboard history (the first time, Windows asks you to turn it on), from which any of the recently copied items can be pasted. Ctrl + V pastes only the latest item.
steps: Clipboard history -> Windows logo key + V
solution.why_others_wrong: Ctrl + V pastes only the most recent item. Windows logo key + C and Ctrl + Shift + C do not open the clipboard history.
solution.final_answer: Option D: Windows logo key + V

fact_checks.claim: Microsoft lists Windows logo key + V as 'Open the clipboard history'.

questions.subject: Computer Knowledge
questions.question_text: On a Linux server, an officer wants to create a new, empty file named audit.log in the current directory. Which command does this when the file does not yet exist?

solution.explanation: touch updates a file's access and modification times; if the named file does not exist, it creates it as an empty file.
steps: touch <file> -> creates an empty file if missing
solution.why_others_wrong: mkdir creates a directory, not a file. rm deletes files. pwd prints the current directory and takes no file name.

fact_checks.claim: touch: 'A FILE argument that does not exist is created empty, unless -c or -h is supplied.'

questions.subject: Computer Knowledge
questions.question_text: Most smartphones on which customers use mobile-banking apps run an operating system developed by Google that is built on the Linux kernel. Which operating system is it?

solution.explanation: Android, developed by Google, is a mobile operating system based on the Linux kernel and is used on most smartphones.
solution.why_others_wrong: iOS is Apple's iPhone operating system. Windows and macOS are desktop operating systems from Microsoft and Apple.

questions.subject: Computer Knowledge
questions.question_text: On a Linux server, the file recon.csv belongs to user asha, but it must now be handed over to user ravi, who takes over the reconciliation work. Which command changes the file's owner?

solution.explanation: chown changes the user and/or group ownership of files: chown ravi recon.csv makes ravi the owner (normally run by root or with sudo).
solution.why_others_wrong: chmod changes permission bits, not the owner. mv renames or moves the file (here to a file named ravi). su switches the user of the shell session.

fact_checks.claim: chown changes the user and/or group ownership of each given file.

questions.subject: Computer Knowledge
questions.question_text: A Linux administrator wants to know how many lines of the log file app.log contain the word FAILED. Which command line prints just that number?

solution.explanation: grep prints only the lines that contain FAILED; the pipe | sends that output to wc -l, which counts newlines, that is, the number of matching lines.
solution.why_others_wrong: > redirects grep's output into a file named wc. wc -l app.log counts ALL lines of the file and grep then searches that count. wc -w counts words and would treat FAILED as a file name.
solution.final_answer: Option D: grep FAILED app.log | wc -l

fact_checks.claim: wc prints newline, word and byte counts; -l, --lines prints the newline counts.

questions.subject: Computer Knowledge
questions.question_text: A branch server's 4 TB disk must be split into six partitions. The technician notes that the older MBR partitioning scheme allows only a few partition-table entries, whereas GPT has no such small limit. How many partition-table entries does an MBR disk support, and what limit does Windows apply to GPT disks?

options.text: MBR: 4 entries (more needs an extended partition); Windows GPT: 128 partitions
MBR: 26 entries, one per drive letter; GPT: unlimited

solution.explanation: An MBR disk has only four partition-table entries; more partitions need an extended partition divided into logical drives. GPT, introduced with UEFI, allows an almost unlimited number by specification, but Windows limits it to 128 partitions. GPT also keeps a backup partition table and CRC32 checks.
solution.why_others_wrong: The other figures are not the MBR and GPT limits; drive letters have nothing to do with partition-table entries.
solution.final_answer: Option A: MBR: 4 entries (more needs an extended partition); Windows GPT: 128 partitions

fact_checks.claim: Microsoft: MBR disks support only four partition table entries; for more, an extended partition is needed. The GPT specification allows an almost unlimited number of partitions, but the Windows implementation restricts this to 128.

questions.subject: Computer Knowledge
questions.question_text: On a shared Linux server, the directory /srv/upload is writable by all users, but officers must not be able to delete or rename one another's files in it. The administrator sets the sticky bit on the directory (chmod +t /srv/upload). What is the effect?

options.text: Every file created in the directory automatically runs with its owner's privileges
A file in the directory can be deleted or renamed only by the file's owner, the directory's owner or root
Files in the directory stay in RAM permanently for faster access
New files in the directory automatically get the directory's group

solution.explanation: On a directory, the sticky bit restricts deletion and renaming: although all users may write into the directory, a file in it can be renamed or deleted only by the owner of the file, the owner of the directory or a privileged process. /tmp is set up the same way.
steps: Sticky bit on a directory -> only owners (or root) can delete or rename entries
solution.why_others_wrong: Running with the owner's privileges is the setuid bit on an executable file. The old meaning of keeping program text in memory does not apply to directories on Linux. Inheriting the directory's group is the setgid bit on a directory.
solution.final_answer: Option B: A file in the directory can be deleted or renamed only by the file's owner, the directory's owner or root

fact_checks.claim: inode(7): in a directory with the sticky bit set, a file can be renamed or deleted only by the owner of the file, by the owner of the directory, and by a privileged process.

questions.subject: Computer Knowledge
questions.question_text: A cash-counter clerk keys in hundreds of amounts a day. To type digits quickly with one hand, she uses the block of number keys on the right side of a full-size keyboard, which works as digits only while a certain lock key is on. What are this block and its lock key called?

solution.explanation: The numeric keypad on the right of a full-size keyboard is laid out like a calculator for fast number entry. When Num Lock is on, its keys type digits; when it is off, they act as cursor and navigation keys.
steps: Calculator-style block on the right -> numeric keypad
solution.why_others_wrong: Function keys are F1 to F12 along the top. Arrow keys move the cursor; Scroll Lock is a different toggle. Caps Lock affects letters, not the number row.
solution.final_answer: Option D: Numeric keypad; Num Lock

questions.subject: Computer Knowledge
questions.question_text: At an enrolment centre, a camera-like device photographs the coloured ring around the pupil of each eye so that a person can later be identified by it. Which input device is this?

solution.explanation: An iris scanner captures the unique pattern of the iris (the coloured ring around the pupil) for biometric identification, alongside fingerprints and face images.
steps: Pattern of the eye's coloured ring -> iris scanner
solution.why_others_wrong: A barcode reader reads printed bar patterns. An OMR reads marked bubbles on forms. A light pen points at or draws on a screen.

questions.subject: Computer Knowledge
questions.question_text: A talking ATM lets a visually impaired customer plug in headphones and hear the on-screen instructions and his balance read out. Which output technology converts the text into spoken words?

solution.explanation: Speech synthesis, or text-to-speech (TTS), produces spoken audio from text and is an OUTPUT technology. Talking ATMs and screen readers use it.
solution.why_others_wrong: Speech recognition is the reverse: spoken words in, text out (input). OCR turns images of text into text. Haptic feedback is vibration, not sound.

questions.subject: Computer Knowledge
questions.question_text: A monochrome laser printer builds each page as a bitmap in its own memory before printing. The printable area is 8 inches x 10 inches, the resolution is 600 dots per inch in both directions, and each dot needs 1 bit (on or off). How much printer memory does one full page bitmap need?

solution.explanation: Dots across = 8 x 600 = 4,800 and down = 10 x 600 = 6,000, so 4,800 x 6,000 = 28,800,000 dots. At 1 bit per dot that is 28,800,000 bits = 28,800,000 / 8 = 3,600,000 bytes (about 3.6 MB).
solution.why_others_wrong: 28,800,000 bytes forgets to divide bits by 8. 86,400,000 bytes assumes 24-bit colour per dot. 450,000 bytes divides by 8 twice.

questions.subject: Computer Knowledge
questions.question_text: A clerk sends a 40-page statement to a slow printer. The computer quickly places the data in a temporary memory area, from which the printer takes it at its own speed, so the clerk can continue working. What is such a temporary holding area called?

solution.explanation: A buffer is a temporary memory area that holds data while it moves between two devices or processes working at different speeds, such as a computer and a printer.
steps: Temporary hold between fast and slow devices -> buffer
solution.why_others_wrong: Registers are tiny storage locations inside the CPU. Virtual memory uses disk space to extend RAM. ROM is permanent read-only memory.

questions.subject: Computer Knowledge
questions.question_text: Main memory (RAM) is divided into millions of storage locations. How does the CPU tell which location it wants to read or write?

options.text: Each location has a unique file name
The CPU searches all locations for the data it needs
Each location is identified by its IP address
Each location has a unique number called its memory address

solution.explanation: Every location (byte) of main memory has a unique numeric address. The CPU puts the address on the address bus to select that location for reading or writing.
steps: Location identified by a number -> memory address
solution.why_others_wrong: File names identify files on storage, not RAM locations. Ordinary RAM is accessed by address, not by searching its contents. IP addresses identify devices on a network.
solution.final_answer: Option D: Each location has a unique number called its memory address

questions.subject: Computer Knowledge
questions.question_text: During a test run, a processor makes 2,000 memory references; 150 of them are NOT found in the cache. What is the cache hit ratio?

solution.explanation: Hits = 2,000 - 150 = 1,850. Hit ratio = hits / total references = 1,850 / 2,000 = 0.925 = 92.5%.
solution.why_others_wrong: 7.5% is the miss ratio. 95% and 85% come from arithmetic slips.

questions.subject: Computer Knowledge
questions.question_text: SSD flash cells can store 1 bit (SLC), 2 bits (MLC), 3 bits (TLC) or 4 bits (QLC) each. For a server that rewrites its log data constantly, which cell type generally offers the highest endurance (number of write/erase cycles), at the highest cost per gigabyte?

solution.explanation: An SLC cell has only two charge levels to tell apart, so it tolerates wear best and lasts the most write/erase cycles; it also stores the fewest bits per cell, which makes it the most expensive per gigabyte. Endurance falls as more bits are packed into each cell (MLC, TLC, QLC).
steps: Fewer levels per cell -> wider margins -> more cycles
solution.why_others_wrong: MLC, TLC and QLC store more bits per cell, which lowers cost per gigabyte but also lowers endurance; QLC has the lowest.

questions.subject: Computer Knowledge
questions.question_text: A 4-way set-associative cache has 256 lines in all, grouped into sets of 4 lines. A main-memory block is placed in set number (block number) mod (number of sets), in any free line of that set. Into which set does block number 1000 go?

solution.explanation: Number of sets = 256 / 4 = 64. Set = 1000 mod 64: 64 x 15 = 960 and 1000 - 960 = 40, so the block goes into set 40 (in any of its 4 lines).
solution.why_others_wrong: 232 is 1000 mod 256, the line number in a direct-mapped cache of 256 lines. 0 is 1000 mod 4 (using the number of ways). 15 is the quotient 1000 / 64, not the remainder.

questions.subject: Computer Knowledge
questions.question_text: A system uses paging with a single-level page table kept in main memory and a TLB (translation lookaside buffer). A TLB lookup takes 10 ns and a main-memory access 100 ns. On a TLB hit, the address is translated and memory is accessed once; on a TLB miss, the page table must first be read from memory and then the data. The TLB hit ratio is 80%. What is the effective memory access time?

solution.concept: Effective access time with a TLB
solution.explanation: Hit: 10 + 100 = 110 ns. Miss: 10 (TLB check) + 100 (page-table entry) + 100 (data) = 210 ns. EAT = 0.8 x 110 + 0.2 x 210 = 88 + 42 = 130 ns.
solution.why_others_wrong: 120 ns leaves out the 10 ns TLB lookup. 110 ns is the hit time only. 210 ns is the miss time only.

questions.subject: Computer Knowledge
questions.question_text: Refer to the DNS records. A PC that has only IPv6 connectivity opens netbanking.bank.example. To which address does it connect?

options.text: 2001:db8:10::25, from the AAAA record of web.bank.example

solution.concept: DNS record types: A and AAAA
solution.explanation: netbanking.bank.example is a CNAME (alias) for web.bank.example. For IPv6 the client asks for the AAAA record, which holds a 128-bit IPv6 address: 2001:db8:10::25. The A record holds the IPv4 address.
solution.why_others_wrong: 203.0.113.25 is the IPv4 address from the A record. The PTR owner name is the IPv4 address reversed, not an address to connect to. NS names the zone's name servers.
solution.final_answer: Option B: 2001:db8:10::25, from the AAAA record of web.bank.example

fact_checks.claim: RFC 3596: the AAAA resource record type stores a single IPv6 address; its type value is 28.

questions.subject: Computer Knowledge
questions.question_text: Refer to the DNS records. A PC's resolver fetches and caches the A record of web.bank.example at 10:00:00. Until what time may it keep answering from its cache without asking the DNS servers again?

solution.explanation: The TTL (time to live) of a resource record is the number of seconds for which it may be cached. The A record's TTL is 300 seconds = 5 minutes, so the cached copy may be used until 10:05:00.
solution.why_others_wrong: 11:00:00 uses the MX records' TTL of 3600 s. 10:00:30 reads 300 as tenths of seconds. The next day uses the NS records' TTL of 86400 s.

fact_checks.claim: RFC 1035: TTL is a 32-bit unsigned integer that specifies the time interval (in seconds) that the resource record may be cached.

questions.subject: Computer Knowledge
questions.question_text: Refer to the DNS records. A customer emails complaints@bank.example and both mail servers are working. To which server will the sending mail server try to deliver first?

options.text: mail1.bank.example, because its preference value 10 is lower
ns1.bank.example, because name servers also accept mail
web.bank.example, because it holds the A record

solution.explanation: Each MX record carries a preference number; lower values are preferred. The sender tries mail1 (10) first and falls back to mail2 (20) only if mail1 cannot be reached.
solution.why_others_wrong: A higher preference number means LOWER priority. Name servers and web servers do not receive mail just because they appear in other records.
solution.final_answer: Option A: mail1.bank.example, because its preference value 10 is lower

fact_checks.claim: RFC 1035: MX PREFERENCE is a 16-bit integer specifying the preference given to this RR among others at the same owner; lower values are preferred.

questions.subject: Computer Knowledge
questions.question_text: Refer to the DNS records. What do the two NS records for bank.example tell other DNS servers?

options.text: That ns1 and ns2 are the bank's mail servers
That ns1.bank.example and ns2.bank.example are the authoritative name servers for the bank.example zone
That ns1 and ns2 are aliases of netbanking.bank.example
That ns1 and ns2 are the IPv6 addresses of the bank's website

solution.explanation: An NS record names a host that is authoritative for the domain: resolvers ask ns1 or ns2 for the official records of bank.example. Two are listed for redundancy.
steps: NS = name server authoritative for the zone
solution.why_others_wrong: Mail servers come from MX records, aliases from CNAME records and IPv6 addresses from AAAA records.
solution.final_answer: Option B: That ns1.bank.example and ns2.bank.example are the authoritative name servers for the bank.example zone

fact_checks.claim: RFC 1035: NS RDATA is a domain name which specifies a host which should be authoritative for the specified class and domain.

questions.subject: Computer Knowledge
questions.question_text: Refer to the DNS records. A firewall log shows only the IP address 203.0.113.25, and an auditor wants the host name that belongs to it. Which lookup gives it, and under which name is the record stored?

options.text: A reverse lookup of the PTR record stored under 25.113.0.203.in-addr.arpa
A forward lookup of the A record stored under 203.0.113.25.in-addr.arpa
A lookup of the CNAME record stored under netbanking.bank.example
A lookup of the MX record stored under bank.example

solution.explanation: Address-to-name mapping uses PTR records in the special in-addr.arpa domain. The four octets of the IPv4 address are written in REVERSE order (25.113.0.203.in-addr.arpa), so that the most general part of the address comes last, as in a domain name. Here it returns web.bank.example.
solution.why_others_wrong: A records map names to addresses (forward lookup), and the octets are not reversed in that option. CNAME and MX records do not map addresses back to names.
solution.final_answer: Option A: A reverse lookup of the PTR record stored under 25.113.0.203.in-addr.arpa

fact_checks.claim: RFC 1035: the IN-ADDR.ARPA domain provides a guaranteed method to perform host address to host name mapping; PTR RDATA is a domain name which points to some location in the domain name space.

questions.subject: Computer Knowledge
questions.question_text: Which network, set up by the US Defense Department's research agency and first connected in 1969 between UCLA and SRI, is regarded as the forerunner of today's internet?

solution.explanation: ARPANET, funded by DARPA (then ARPA), sent its first computer-to-computer message in 1969 between UCLA and SRI. It used packet switching and evolved into the internet in the early 1980s.
steps: 1969, US defence research agency, forerunner of the internet -> ARPANET
solution.why_others_wrong: Ethernet is a LAN technology. NICNET was India's National Informatics Centre network. Usenet is a discussion-group system that came later.

fact_checks.claim: DARPA: the roots of the modern internet lie in DARPA's work begun in the 1960s; ARPANET launched in 1969 with the first computer-to-computer signal between UCLA and SRI and by 1983 had evolved into the internet.

questions.subject: Computer Knowledge
questions.question_text: Who invented the World Wide Web in 1989 while working at CERN, the European physics laboratory?

solution.explanation: Tim Berners-Lee, a British scientist, proposed and built the World Wide Web at CERN, starting in 1989; by the end of 1990 the first web server and browser were running there.
solution.why_others_wrong: Vint Cerf co-designed the TCP/IP protocols. Bill Gates co-founded Microsoft. Ray Tomlinson sent the first network email and chose the @ sign.

fact_checks.claim: CERN: Tim Berners-Lee, a British scientist, invented the World Wide Web (WWW) in 1989, while working at CERN.

questions.subject: Computer Knowledge
questions.question_text: Bank staff keep their procedure manual on an internal website where any authorised employee can edit pages directly in the browser, and every change is saved in the page history. What is such a collaboratively edited website called?

solution.explanation: A wiki is a website whose pages many users can create and edit through the browser, with a history of every change. Wikipedia is the best-known example.
steps: Many users edit pages + history -> wiki
solution.why_others_wrong: A blog is a series of dated posts usually written by one author or a small team. A search engine finds pages. A payment portal processes transactions.

questions.subject: Computer Knowledge
questions.question_text: A customer opens the bank's website, which runs behind a reverse proxy. The proxy is working, but the application server behind it has crashed, so the proxy cannot get a valid response from it. Which HTTP status code does the proxy most likely return?

solution.explanation: 502 Bad Gateway means that a server acting as a gateway or proxy received an invalid response from the upstream server it contacted while trying to fulfil the request.
solution.why_others_wrong: 404 means the resource was not found. 401 means valid credentials are missing. 301 is a permanent redirect. None of them describes a failed upstream server.

questions.subject: Computer Knowledge
questions.question_text: An officer searches for jaguar insurance but keeps getting pages about the car brand. In a search engine such as Google, how should she leave out pages containing the word car?

solution.explanation: Putting a minus sign directly in front of a word (-car) tells the search engine to leave out results that contain that word.
solution.why_others_wrong: +car does not exclude anything. site: limits results to a website or domain. Quotation marks search for the exact phrase, which would include car.

fact_checks.claim: Google Search Help: enter - in front of a word that you want to leave out, for example jaguar speed -car.

questions.subject: Computer Knowledge
questions.question_text: A net-banking site sets its session cookie with the attribute SameSite=Strict. A customer who is already logged in clicks a link to the bank's site from an email-provider web page (a different site). What happens to the session cookie on that first request?

options.text: The browser sends it, because the link opens the bank's own address
The browser sends it only if the link uses HTTP rather than HTTPS
The browser does not send it, because the request comes from another site; the customer may have to log in again

solution.explanation: With SameSite=Strict, a cookie is sent only on requests that originate from the same site that set it. A navigation started from another site is cross-site, so the cookie is withheld; this blocks cross-site request forgery (CSRF) at the cost of sometimes asking the user to log in again. SameSite=Lax would send it on such top-level navigations with safe methods like GET.
steps: Link from another site = cross-site -> cookie not sent
solution.why_others_wrong: Sending it on cross-site top-level navigation is Lax behaviour, not Strict. SameSite has nothing to do with HTTP versus HTTPS (and secure session cookies are not sent over plain HTTP at all). The cookie is not deleted; it is simply not attached to that request.
solution.final_answer: Option C: The browser does not send it, because the request comes from another site; the customer may have to log in again

fact_checks.claim: MDN Set-Cookie: SameSite=Strict sends the cookie only for requests originating from the same site that set the cookie; Lax also sends it for cross-site top-level navigations that use a safe method.

questions.subject: Computer Knowledge
questions.question_text: A payment API may resend a request automatically after a network timeout. Under HTTP semantics, which group of request methods is defined as IDEMPOTENT, so that sending the same request several times has the same intended effect on the server as sending it once?

solution.explanation: RFC 9110 defines PUT, DELETE and the safe methods (GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, TRACE) as idempotent. POST is not: repeating a POST may, for example, create two payments. That is why APIs that retry POST requests use idempotency keys.
steps: Idempotent = PUT, DELETE + safe methods (GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, TRACE)
solution.why_others_wrong: POST is not idempotent, so every option that contains it is wrong; PATCH is not defined as idempotent either.
solution.final_answer: Option D: GET, HEAD, PUT and DELETE

fact_checks.claim: RFC 9110 section 9.2.2: PUT, DELETE, and safe request methods are idempotent.

questions.subject: Computer Knowledge
questions.question_text: In a small branch, five PCs share files and a printer directly with one another; there is no dedicated server, and every PC can act both as a client and as a server. What type of network is this?

solution.explanation: In a peer-to-peer network, all computers have equal status and share their resources directly, each acting as both client and server. A client-server network has dedicated servers that provide services to clients.
steps: No dedicated server, equal computers -> peer-to-peer
solution.why_others_wrong: Client-server needs a dedicated server. A MAN covers a city. A VPN is an encrypted tunnel over another network.

questions.subject: Computer Knowledge
questions.question_text: During a power cut, a branch officer shares her phone's mobile-data connection over Wi-Fi so that her laptop can reach the internet. What is this feature called?

solution.explanation: A mobile hotspot (tethering) turns the phone into a small wireless router that shares its mobile-data internet connection with other devices over Wi-Fi (or USB or Bluetooth).
steps: Phone shares its data connection with a laptop -> hotspot / tethering
solution.why_others_wrong: Bluetooth pairing only links two devices. Airplane mode switches the radios off. NFC is used for contactless payments over a few centimetres.

questions.subject: Computer Knowledge
questions.question_text: A bank's new application server listens on TCP port 8443. According to the IANA port ranges, ports 0 to 1023 are the System (well-known) Ports. To which range does 8443 belong?

options.text: It is not a valid port number

solution.explanation: RFC 6335 divides the 16-bit port space into System Ports 0-1023, User (registered) Ports 1024-49151 and Dynamic (private or ephemeral) Ports 49152-65535. 8443 lies in 1024-49151.
solution.why_others_wrong: 8443 is above 1023 and below 49152. Port numbers go up to 65535, so 8443 is valid.

fact_checks.claim: RFC 6335: System Ports (Well Known Ports) 0-1023, User Ports (Registered Ports) 1024-49151, Dynamic (Private/Ephemeral) Ports 49152-65535.

questions.subject: Computer Knowledge
questions.question_text: A network engineer sees an unknown device with MAC address 00:1A:2B:3C:4D:5E on a branch switch and looks up the first three bytes, 00:1A:2B, in the IEEE registry. What do these 24 bits identify?

options.text: The switch port the device is connected to
The organisation (manufacturer) to which that block of addresses was assigned - the OUI

solution.explanation: A 48-bit MAC address (EUI-48) is made of a 24-bit Organizationally Unique Identifier (OUI) assigned by the IEEE to the organisation, followed by 24 bits assigned by that organisation. Looking up the OUI reveals the vendor.
solution.why_others_wrong: MAC addresses do not contain IP subnets or switch-port numbers. The last 24 bits, not the first, are chosen by the maker for each interface.
solution.final_answer: Option C: The organisation (manufacturer) to which that block of addresses was assigned - the OUI

fact_checks.claim: IEEE: the OUI included in an MA-L assignment may be appended with 24 organization-supplied bits to form an EUI-48; the MA-L was previously referred to as an OUI.

questions.subject: Computer Knowledge
questions.question_text: A branch on a long leased line sends 1,000-byte frames over a 1 Mbps link using stop-and-wait: after each frame it waits for an acknowledgement before sending the next. The one-way propagation delay is 4 ms. Ignoring the time to transmit the acknowledgement and any processing delay, what is the link utilisation (efficiency)?

solution.explanation: Frame transmission time = 1,000 x 8 bits / 1,000,000 bps = 8 ms. After sending, the sender waits for the frame to arrive (4 ms) and the acknowledgement to return (4 ms). Each cycle is 8 + 2 x 4 = 16 ms, of which the link is busy for 8 ms: efficiency = 8 / 16 = 50%.
solution.why_others_wrong: 66.7% counts the propagation delay only once (8 / 12). 100% ignores the waiting. 33.3% doubles the frame time as well.

questions.subject: Computer Knowledge
questions.question_text: An IPv4 datagram of 4,000 bytes (a 20-byte header plus 3,980 bytes of data) must cross a link whose MTU is 1,500 bytes, so a router fragments it. Each fragment gets its own 20-byte header, and the fragment-offset field counts in units of 8 bytes. What is the fragment-offset field value of the THIRD fragment?

solution.explanation: Each fragment can carry 1,500 - 20 = 1,480 bytes of data (a multiple of 8). The fragments carry 1,480, 1,480 and 1,020 bytes. The third starts at data byte 2,960, and the offset field stores 2,960 / 8 = 370.
solution.why_others_wrong: 185 is the offset of the second fragment. 2,960 is the offset in bytes, not in 8-byte units. 3 is the fragment's position, not its offset.

fact_checks.claim: RFC 791: the fragment offset is measured in units of 8 octets (64 bits).

questions.subject: Computer Knowledge
questions.question_text: A customer gets an email saying he has won Rs 25 lakh in an international lottery he never entered, and that he must first pay a 'processing fee' of Rs 15,000 to release the prize. What is this?

solution.explanation: Advance-fee frauds promise a large reward (a lottery win, inheritance or loan) but first demand a smaller 'fee', 'tax' or 'charge'. Once paid, the fraudster asks for more or disappears; the prize does not exist. A lottery one never entered cannot be won.
steps: Unexpected prize + pay a fee first -> advance-fee fraud
solution.why_others_wrong: Genuine prizes do not require upfront fees, and one cannot win a lottery one did not enter. The email has nothing to do with software updates or flooding a server.

questions.subject: Computer Knowledge
questions.question_text: A customer searches the internet for her bank's customer-care number, calls the first number shown on a random website, and the 'executive' asks her to share the OTP to 'reverse a failed transaction'. What is the safest practice?

options.text: Share the OTP, because she called the number herself
Share only half of the OTP to be safe
Ask the caller to send his employee ID before sharing the OTP
Take customer-care numbers only from the bank's official website, app, card or passbook, and never share an OTP with anyone

solution.explanation: Fraudsters publish fake helpline numbers on websites, listings and social media. Contact details should be taken only from official sources, and an OTP must never be shared with anyone, because it authorises a transaction.
steps: Number from an unofficial page -> may be fake
solution.why_others_wrong: Calling the number yourself does not make it genuine. Part of an OTP or an 'employee ID' from the caller gives no protection; any ID can be invented.
solution.final_answer: Option D: Take customer-care numbers only from the bank's official website, app, card or passbook, and never share an OTP with anyone

questions.subject: Computer Knowledge
questions.question_text: A malicious website loads the bank's real fund-transfer page in an invisible frame and places a 'Claim your reward' button exactly over the hidden 'Confirm transfer' button. The user thinks he is clicking the reward button. What is this attack called?

solution.explanation: Clickjacking hides or disguises a legitimate page under layers so that a user's click lands on a control of that page without his knowledge. Sites defend against it by forbidding other sites from framing them with the Content-Security-Policy frame-ancestors directive (or the older X-Frame-Options header).
steps: Invisible frame + decoy button -> hijacked click -> clickjacking
solution.why_others_wrong: SQL injection attacks a database through input fields. Pharming redirects users through tampered DNS. Keylogging records keystrokes.

fact_checks.claim: OWASP describes clickjacking as a 'UI redress attack' and recommends the CSP frame-ancestors directive, with X-Frame-Options for older browsers.

questions.subject: Computer Knowledge
questions.question_text: An officer merely opens a compromised news website in an outdated browser and, without clicking any download or approving anything, malware is silently installed by exploiting a browser flaw. What is this called?

solution.explanation: In a drive-by download, malicious code on a web page exploits a vulnerability in the browser or a plug-in to install malware simply because the page was visited. Keeping browsers patched is the main defence.
steps: Just visiting a page + exploit + silent install -> drive-by download
solution.why_others_wrong: Baiting leaves an infected item (such as a USB drive) for a victim to use. A logic bomb waits for a condition inside a system. Typosquatting registers misspelt domain names.

questions.subject: Computer Knowledge
questions.question_text: At a crowded railway station, an attacker exploits a weakness in a traveller's phone's Bluetooth to copy his contacts, messages and photos without his knowledge. What is this Bluetooth attack called?

solution.explanation: Bluesnarfing is the theft of data from a device over a Bluetooth connection without the owner's permission. Bluejacking only sends unsolicited messages to nearby Bluetooth devices.
solution.why_others_wrong: Bluejacking sends unwanted messages but does not steal data. Smishing is SMS phishing. Juice jacking attacks phones through tampered USB charging ports.

questions.subject: Computer Knowledge
questions.question_text: A phishing link shows a domain that looks exactly like bank.example, but its letter 'a' is actually the Cyrillic letter 'а', which looks identical on screen, so it is a different domain owned by the fraudster. What is this technique called?

solution.explanation: Internationalised domain names (IDNs) can contain letters from other scripts. A homograph attack registers a domain whose characters look identical to a genuine one, such as a Cyrillic 'а' in place of the Latin 'a', so even a careful reader cannot spot the difference.
steps: Look-alike characters from another script -> IDN homograph attack
solution.why_others_wrong: Typosquatting relies on visible misspellings or typing mistakes. Session hijacking steals an active session. A brute-force attack tries many passwords.

questions.subject: Computer Knowledge
questions.question_text: In a classroom RSA example, p = 3 and q = 11, so n = 33 and phi(n) = (p - 1)(q - 1) = 20. The public exponent is e = 3. The private exponent d is the smallest positive number with (e x d) mod phi(n) = 1. What is d?

solution.explanation: We need 3d mod 20 = 1. Trying d = 1, 2, ...: 3 x 7 = 21 = 20 + 1, so d = 7. Check: encrypting 4 gives 4^3 mod 33 = 64 mod 33 = 31, and 31^7 mod 33 = 4, the original message.
solution.why_others_wrong: 3 is e itself (3 x 3 = 9). 11 solves 3d = 1 mod 32, using n - 1 instead of phi(n). 13 gives 3 x 13 = 39 = 19 mod 20.

questions.subject: Computer Knowledge
questions.question_text: A developer encrypts a bank's image of a cheque with AES in ECB (Electronic Codebook) mode, and the outline of the cheque is still visible in the encrypted image. Why does this happen?

options.text: ECB encrypts each block independently with the same key, so identical plaintext blocks give identical ciphertext blocks and patterns remain visible
AES is a weak algorithm that does not really encrypt image data
ECB mode leaves every second block unencrypted
ECB uses a different random key for each block, which distorts but does not hide the image

solution.explanation: In ECB, every block is encrypted separately with the same key and no chaining or nonce, so repeated plaintext blocks (large areas of the same colour) produce repeated ciphertext blocks and the data's structure stays visible. Modes such as CBC, CTR or GCM mix in an IV, nonce or counter to hide such patterns.
steps: Same plaintext block -> same ciphertext block
solution.why_others_wrong: AES itself is strong; the weakness lies in the mode. ECB encrypts every block. It uses one key for all blocks, not a random key per block.
solution.final_answer: Option A: ECB encrypts each block independently with the same key, so identical plaintext blocks give identical ciphertext blocks and patterns remain visible

fact_checks.claim: ECB fails to hide data patterns because it encrypts identical plaintext blocks into identical ciphertext blocks.
NIST SP 800-38A defines five confidentiality modes for block ciphers: ECB, CBC, CFB, OFB and CTR.

questions.subject: Computer Knowledge
questions.question_text: A bank's server private key is stolen in 2026. Its old TLS 1.3 sessions recorded by an attacker in 2025 still cannot be decrypted, because each session's key was agreed with fresh (ephemeral) Diffie-Hellman values that were discarded afterwards. Which property is this?

solution.explanation: With forward secrecy, session keys are derived from ephemeral key-exchange values that are thrown away after use, so compromising the long-term private key later does not reveal past session keys. TLS 1.3 removed static RSA key exchange, so all its public-key based key exchanges provide forward secrecy.
steps: Ephemeral DH per session + long-term key stolen later -> past sessions safe
solution.why_others_wrong: Non-repudiation stops a signer from denying a signature. Key escrow deposits keys with a third party. Certificate pinning makes an app accept only specific certificates.
solution.final_answer: Option C: Forward secrecy (perfect forward secrecy)

fact_checks.claim: RFC 8446 (TLS 1.3): static RSA and Diffie-Hellman cipher suites have been removed; all public-key based key exchange mechanisms now provide forward secrecy.

questions.subject: Computer Knowledge
questions.question_text: A bank and a payment partner share a secret key. Every API message carries a tag computed from the message and the secret key with SHA-256, so the receiver can confirm the message was not altered and that it came from someone holding the key. What is this mechanism?

solution.explanation: HMAC combines a cryptographic hash function such as SHA-256 with a shared secret key. Only holders of the key can compute a valid tag, so it proves both integrity and the origin of the message. A plain hash proves neither against an attacker, who can recompute it after changing the message.
solution.why_others_wrong: A plain SHA-256 checksum has no key, so an attacker can alter the message and recompute it. Public-key encryption gives confidentiality and uses key pairs, not a shared secret. Base64 is only an encoding.
solution.final_answer: Option B: HMAC (hash-based message authentication code)

fact_checks.claim: RFC 2104 describes HMAC, a mechanism for message authentication using cryptographic hash functions with a secret shared key.

questions.subject: Computer Knowledge
questions.question_text:
Refer to the Cheques table. What does this query return?

SELECT MIN(amount) FROM Cheques WHERE status = 'Returned';

solution.explanation: WHERE keeps only the returned cheques, C102 (48,000) and C106 (9,000). MIN returns the smaller amount, 9,000.
solution.why_others_wrong: 48,000 is the MAX of the returned cheques. 12,000 is the smallest pending cheque. 57,000 is the SUM of the returned cheques.

questions.subject: Computer Knowledge
questions.question_text:
Refer to the Cheques table. How many rows does this statement change?

UPDATE Cheques SET status = 'Cleared' WHERE status = 'Pending';

solution.explanation: UPDATE changes only the rows that satisfy WHERE. Two rows are Pending (C103 and C108), so 2 rows become Cleared; the others are untouched.
solution.why_others_wrong: 3 would also include the NULL row C107, which does not equal 'Pending'. 8 is what happens if the WHERE clause is left out. 1 counts only one account (A1), but UPDATE works on rows.

questions.subject: Computer Knowledge
questions.question_text:
Refer to the Cheques table. What does this query return?

SELECT acc_no FROM Cheques WHERE status = 'Cleared'
INTERSECT
SELECT acc_no FROM Cheques WHERE status = 'Returned';

solution.explanation: The first query gives the accounts with a cleared cheque: A1, A3, A2. The second gives the accounts with a returned cheque: A2, A4. INTERSECT keeps only values in both (without duplicates): A2.
solution.why_others_wrong: A1 has no returned cheque. A4 has no cleared cheque. Listing all four accounts is UNION, not INTERSECT.

questions.subject: Computer Knowledge
questions.question_text:
Refer to the Cheques table. What does this query return?

SELECT COUNT(*) FROM Cheques WHERE status <> 'Cleared';

solution.explanation: Rows that are not Cleared are C102, C103, C106 and C108 (4 rows). C107 has a NULL status: NULL <> 'Cleared' evaluates to UNKNOWN, not TRUE, so WHERE drops that row too. The answer is 4.
solution.why_others_wrong: 5 wrongly counts the NULL row. 3 is the number of Cleared rows. 8 is the whole table.
